claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers is governed by interface-mediated dislocation dynamics.
Compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and local short-range order at the interfaces create heterogeneous obstacles.
These heterogeneous interfacial obstacles foster dislocation nucleation and pileup.
Interfacial dislocation nucleation and pileup promote gradual creep-strain accumulation.
The as-deposited interfaces contain significant compositional complexity, lattice distortion, and short-range-ordered zones.
Post-deposition annealing or adjusted deposition parameters can alter short-range order and interface coherence while preserving the nanoscale multilayer architecture.
Local compositional fluctuations and short-range order at multilayer interfaces influence dislocation nucleation and mobility.
Sustained loading concentrates stress at complex FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy interfaces.
Local lattice distortions and compositional inhomogeneities cause preferential activation of dislocation sources at the interfaces.
Interfacial dislocation pileups eventually trigger interface sliding and plastic flow.
Increasing coherent interfacial ordering reduces the density and activity of dislocation nucleation sites.
An interface-ordered multilayer will have a lower creep rate than the as-deposited baseline.
The non-optimized, disordered interfaces in the as-deposited baseline permit significant dislocation nucleation and pileup under sustained load.
The proposed mechanism is limited to nanoscale multilayer coatings containing high-entropy alloys with FCC/BCC phases.
The proposed mechanism may not extend to conventional, single-phase, or thicker metallic coatings.
The predicted effects apply under inert testing conditions and at temperatures where creep processes dominate.
Grain-boundary diffusion may contribute to creep as a competing mechanism.
